title: Your Soft Skills Baseline — Professional Edition
theme: Workplace leadership, team dynamics, ethical decisions, and strategic thinking
description: 10 real workplace situations to measure how you naturally lead, decide, and collaborate under pressure. No right or wrong — your honest responses create the most useful profile. Takes about 15 minutes.
target_audience: Working professionals, HR, trainers, and managers (ages 26+)
learning_objectives: Establish your professional baseline across 8 key dimensions
Understand how you naturally respond under workplace pressure
Identify your leadership strengths and areas for professional growth
how_to_play: Read each scenario carefully and choose the response that feels most like what you would actually do — not what you think is the 'right' answer. Your honest choices create the most useful baseline.
psychological_framework: Situational judgment assessment based on behavioural decision theory and professional leadership research

glossary_terms.definition: The process of choosing between different options after considering their consequences
Giving up one thing to gain another — every choice has a cost
A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term goal
The result or outcome of a choice or action
A particular way of looking at something — everyone has a different perspective

rounds.title: The Underperforming Team Member
rounds.story: Your team member has been underperforming for 2 months. They used to be your best performer — consistently delivering high-quality work and often helping others. HR wants you to put them on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP). You haven't had a direct conversation with them yet.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle this situation before involving HR further
rounds.coaching_moment: How a manager responds to a sudden dip in a previously strong performer says a great deal about whether they lead with data or assumptions — and whether they see people as resources to manage or humans to understand.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time you managed or witnessed a performance decline. Was the root cause ever different from the initial assumption?

choices.label: Have a direct but private conversation first — understand what changed before involving HR
choices.feedback: A strong performer who suddenly declines almost always has an identifiable cause — personal stress, misalignment, unclear expectations, or something outside work. Talking first is both the human and the strategic choice: you get better information, and you give the person a chance to self-correct before the formal process creates defensiveness.
choices.coaching_moment: A PIP for a previously high performer without a conversation first is a failure of management, not a solution to it. Data before process — always.

choices.label: Follow HR's guidance and initiate the PIP — the process exists for a reason
choices.feedback: Process matters — but process applied without judgment causes real damage. Initiating a PIP on a formerly strong performer without first understanding what happened signals to the team that past performance earns no grace. It also makes it harder for the person to recover, because the formal process adds anxiety on top of whatever was already affecting them.
choices.coaching_moment: HR processes are tools, not substitutes for leadership judgment. The process is there for when conversations fail — not instead of them.

choices.label: Redistribute their critical work to others to protect delivery, and monitor the situation quietly
choices.feedback: Quietly redistributing work protects short-term delivery but doesn't address the person or their situation. The team will notice the reallocation and draw their own conclusions. Meanwhile, the underlying cause remains unaddressed and will likely worsen. You've protected output but not the person or the relationship.
choices.coaching_moment: Protecting delivery by avoiding the harder conversation is not management — it's delay with compounding interest.

rounds.image_prompt: manager in a quiet meeting room having a thoughtful one-on-one conversation with a team member who looks stressed
rounds.scene_hint: corporate office, private meeting, empathy and directness in the air

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Stolen Credit
rounds.story: In an important meeting, a senior colleague presents your analysis — the research, the framework, the conclusions — as their own work. Your manager doesn't know who created it. The senior colleague doesn't correct the impression. You are sitting in the same room.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond in this situation
rounds.coaching_moment: Credit appropriation by senior colleagues is one of the most common and hardest-to-navigate professional situations. How you respond reveals your resilience, your political intelligence, and how you value your own work.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has your work ever been presented without attribution? What did you do, and what did it cost you to stay silent — or to speak?

choices.label: Speak up in the moment — calmly add context that makes your contribution visible without direct accusation
choices.feedback: Speaking in the moment is difficult but often most effective. A calm, non-accusatory contribution — 'I can add some context on the methodology I used here' — makes your role visible without creating a confrontation. It also signals to the room, including your manager, that you have direct knowledge of this work.
choices.coaching_moment: The window to reclaim credit in a meeting closes fast. A calm, professional addition is far more powerful than silence followed by a complaint after the fact.

choices.label: Speak to your manager privately after the meeting and clarify who did the work
choices.feedback: Following up privately with your manager is a reasonable alternative if speaking in the meeting feels too risky. It's honest, professional, and gives your manager accurate information without a public confrontation. The downside is that the impression is already formed in the room — correction is harder after the fact.
choices.coaching_moment: Private correction works best when you have a strong relationship with your manager and can frame the conversation around the work, not the person.

choices.label: Say nothing now — it's not worth the political cost, and your manager will eventually know
choices.feedback: Staying silent protects you from short-term conflict but reinforces a pattern where your work is available for appropriation with no consequence. The belief that your manager will 'eventually know' is usually optimistic — attribution of credit rarely self-corrects. The political cost of staying silent compounds over time.
choices.coaching_moment: Silence in the face of misattribution isn't neutrality — it's acceptance. The cost appears slowly but is real.

rounds.image_prompt: professional in a boardroom looking composed while a senior colleague presents at the front, projection screen visible
rounds.scene_hint: corporate meeting room, moment of credit being taken, decision under social pressure

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Impossible Deadline
rounds.story: Your manager has just committed to a client deadline that you know — based on your team's current capacity and complexity of the work — is not achievable. The client heard the commitment and nodded. You are sitting in the room and your manager looks relieved the client accepted.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle this situation
rounds.coaching_moment: Upward management — the ability to give your manager accurate information even when it is inconvenient — is one of the most underdeveloped professional skills. The moment to act is almost always earlier than feels comfortable.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has your team ever been committed to a deadline without your input? What happened to the work and to the team's morale?

choices.label: Speak to your manager privately right after the meeting — share your assessment honestly and offer a revised timeline
choices.feedback: Flagging the problem immediately — before the team has been briefed, before expectations have calcified — is the highest-value move. You give your manager the information they need to manage the client relationship before delivery fails. The discomfort of that conversation is far smaller than the cost of a missed deadline.
choices.coaching_moment: The best time to surface a delivery risk is the moment you identify it, not after the team has worked themselves to exhaustion on an impossible schedule.

choices.label: Push the team hard and try to meet the deadline — the commitment has been made
choices.feedback: Treating an unrealistic commitment as fixed is a loyalty instinct, not a strategic one. Pushing the team toward an unachievable deadline without flagging the risk destroys morale, degrades quality, and almost always results in a missed deadline anyway — but now without the goodwill buffer you would have had by flagging it early.
choices.coaching_moment: Protecting your manager from uncomfortable information is not loyalty — it's the most expensive kind of deference. Accurate information, delivered early, is the most valuable thing a manager can receive.

choices.label: Raise it in front of the client in the meeting — correct the expectation immediately
choices.feedback: Speaking up in front of the client is brave but usually counterproductive. It undermines your manager's credibility in front of the client and creates conflict in the room that damages the relationship. The right audience for this information is your manager, privately, not the client, publicly.
choices.coaching_moment: Correcting your manager in front of a client is almost never the right move — even when you're right. The forum matters as much as the information.

rounds.image_prompt: professional in a client meeting looking concerned, manager and client shaking hands in background
rounds.scene_hint: corporate client meeting, delivery commitment just made, silent concern

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Budget Integrity Test
rounds.story: Midway through executing your project, you find a way to save 20% of the budget without compromising outcomes — better vendor terms, a more efficient approach than planned. Your company's culture has an unwritten rule: spend your full budget or risk getting a smaller allocation next year. Your finance contact confirms this happens.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the savings
rounds.coaching_moment: Budget integrity — choosing what is right for the organisation over what is safe for your own resource position — is a direct test of ethical reasoning and long-term strategic thinking in professional environments.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever spent budget you didn't need to protect your allocation? What would a more honest version of that decision have looked like?

choices.label: Report the savings, flag the systemic incentive problem, and let leadership decide how to use the surplus
choices.feedback: Returning savings and flagging the cultural misalignment is the highest-integrity response. It serves the organisation, demonstrates trustworthiness, and — critically — names the systemic problem rather than silently perpetuating it. Leaders who do this earn a rare kind of credibility with finance and senior leadership.
choices.coaching_moment: The instinct to spend the full budget to 'protect' next year's allocation is almost universal — and almost universally wrong. The organisations that change are led by people willing to name the bad incentive out loud.

choices.label: Spend the remaining budget on 'future proofing' — equipment, training, or reserves that could be useful later
choices.feedback: Spending budget on things you don't currently need in order to avoid returning it is a rationalisation that most finance teams see through. It misallocates resources, signals that your budget requests can't be trusted, and makes next year's negotiation harder — not easier — once finance has seen the pattern.
choices.coaching_moment: Discretionary spending at end-of-budget is one of the most common forms of organisational waste. Rationalising it as 'investment' doesn't change what it is.

choices.label: Return the savings quietly without flagging the budget culture issue — just do the right thing for now
choices.feedback: Returning savings is better than spending unnecessarily — it's the honest choice. But doing it quietly, without flagging the incentive problem that makes honesty feel risky for most people, misses an opportunity to create systemic change. The right thing done without naming the wrong system doesn't improve the system.
choices.coaching_moment: Individual integrity is necessary but not sufficient. The most impactful professionals don't just do the right thing — they make it easier for others to do the right thing too.

rounds.image_prompt: finance professional reviewing budget spreadsheet showing savings, looking thoughtful in a modern office
rounds.scene_hint: corporate office, budget review, ethical crossroads

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Team Conflict
rounds.story: Two of your best team members — both high performers — have a significant personality clash that is affecting delivery timelines and the morale of the wider team. They have both separately come to you and asked you to resolve the situation in their favour. Each is convinced they are right and the other is the problem.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle this conflict
rounds.coaching_moment: How a leader navigates a conflict where both parties are valued and both feel wronged is one of the most practical tests of leadership maturity. The answer is almost never to pick a side.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a workplace conflict you witnessed or were involved in. Was the resolution imposed or owned? Which lasted?

choices.label: Meet with each person individually first, then bring them together with a clear mediation structure
choices.feedback: Individual conversations first allow you to understand each perspective without the defensiveness that group settings trigger. Bringing them together with a structure — not as judge, but as facilitator — creates the conditions for a resolution they own rather than one imposed on them. Owned resolutions last; imposed ones rarely do.
choices.coaching_moment: The most durable team conflict resolutions are not adjudications — they're structured conversations where both parties arrive at shared understanding without either side needing to fully 'win'.

choices.label: Tell both of them that professional behaviour is non-negotiable and the conflict must not affect delivery
choices.feedback: Setting the expectation that professional behaviour is required is correct — but stating the rule without creating the conditions for the conflict to actually resolve is a managerial shortcut. They already know the behaviour is unacceptable; what they need is a structured path to resolution. Rules without process leave the conflict intact.
choices.coaching_moment: Telling people what to do is leadership; creating the conditions for them to do it is management. Both are necessary.

choices.label: Separate their workstreams structurally so they don't need to interact closely
choices.feedback: Structural separation reduces immediate friction but entrenches the conflict and removes two of your best people from full contribution. It also signals to both of them — and to the rest of the team — that you managed around the problem rather than through it. In a small or medium team, there are rarely enough workstreams to keep this sustainable.
choices.coaching_moment: Avoidance through structure is a common and understandable choice — but it accumulates. The conflict you don't resolve today becomes the team dysfunction you manage tomorrow.

rounds.image_prompt: manager sitting across from two team members having a structured three-way conversation in a glass meeting room
rounds.scene_hint: team conflict, mediation, professional tension, solution-finding

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Promotion Politics
rounds.story: You learn from a source you trust that a colleague you respect is being overlooked for a well-deserved promotion — not because of performance, but because they don't have visibility with a key decision-maker. You have a good relationship with that decision-maker and could raise it. Your colleague hasn't asked you to intervene.
rounds.goal: Decide whether and how to act
rounds.coaching_moment: Using influence proactively on behalf of someone who hasn't asked you to is one of the highest forms of professional advocacy — and also one of the most politically complex. The right move depends on your reading of the situation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has anyone ever advocated for you without being asked? What did it mean to you? Have you done it for someone else?

choices.label: Tell your colleague what you've heard and ask if they would like you to raise it on their behalf
choices.feedback: Telling your colleague first respects their agency and gives them the information they need to make their own choices. They may want you to raise it, handle it themselves, or choose not to act at all. Checking before acting treats them as a full participant in the situation, not just its subject.
choices.coaching_moment: Advocacy without the person's knowledge or consent — even well-intentioned — can undermine their autonomy and, if it goes wrong, create awkwardness they weren't prepared for. Ask first.

choices.label: Raise it directly with the decision-maker — you know the colleague is deserving and waiting costs them
choices.feedback: Acting without asking is well-intentioned and may work — but it bypasses your colleague's autonomy. If it goes well, they benefit. If it creates complications — the decision-maker asks them about it, or the conversation doesn't go as planned — they're in a situation you created without their consent. The instinct is good; the sequence needs refinement.
choices.coaching_moment: The impulse to act is admirable. The best version of that impulse includes a five-minute conversation with the person you're trying to help before you act on their behalf.

choices.label: Stay out of it — office politics isn't your business and intervening could backfire for both of you
choices.feedback: The caution is understandable — advocacy does carry risk. But 'it could backfire' is almost always a rationalisation for inaction in situations that require courage. Watching a deserving colleague get passed over without using the influence you have is a choice — it's just a passive one, and passive choices have costs too.
choices.coaching_moment: The question is not whether advocacy carries risk — it does. The question is whether the risk of inaction is lower. Often it isn't.

rounds.image_prompt: professional having a private conversation over coffee with a colleague, listening carefully
rounds.scene_hint: office corridor or café, colleague advocacy, professional loyalty

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Company Loyalty vs. Opportunity
rounds.story: A competitor has just offered you a 40% salary jump with a strong role. You'd likely take it if the timing were different — but your current company sponsored an expensive professional certification program you completed 3 months ago. Your contract has no explicit bond clause, but the intent was always that you'd apply the skills here.
rounds.goal: Decide how to approach this decision
rounds.coaching_moment: Balancing personal financial interest against an implicit professional obligation is a test of delayed gratification, ethical reasoning, and how you reason about trust — both what you owe and what you're owed.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When have you stayed somewhere longer than you wanted to? When have you left faster than felt right? What guided those decisions?

choices.label: Have an honest conversation with your current employer — share the offer, give them a chance to respond, and make a decision from a place of full information
choices.feedback: Transparency with your current employer — using the offer as leverage for an honest conversation about your value — is both ethically sound and strategically intelligent. It gives your employer the information they need to retain you if they want to, and it gives you data about how they value you. The outcome may be the same, but the process treats the relationship honestly.
choices.coaching_moment: Using an outside offer to have a direct conversation about your value is not betrayal — it's honesty. Most organisations prefer an honest conversation to a sudden resignation.

choices.label: Commit to staying for at least 12 more months to honour the implied obligation before reconsidering
choices.feedback: Deciding to honour the implied obligation is a reasonable ethical position — especially if you made an unspoken commitment when accepting the certification. Staying and applying the skills makes good on that understanding. The financial cost is real, but the reputational and personal integrity cost of leaving immediately is also real.
choices.coaching_moment: Implicit obligations are less enforceable than explicit ones but no less real. Whether you honour them tells you — and those around you — something important about what kind of professional you are.

choices.label: Take the offer — the market pays what it pays, and the absence of a bond clause makes it legally clean
choices.feedback: The absence of a bond clause makes this legally permissible — but professional relationships run on implied trust as much as written contracts. Leaving immediately after a significant employer investment, without a conversation, is a signal the industry notices. It's not catastrophic, but it is a data point that follows you.
choices.coaching_moment: Legal permission and ethical soundness are not the same thing. The strongest careers are built on a reputation that exceeds what's contractually required.

rounds.image_prompt: professional looking at two paths — current office building and a new company logo — thoughtfully weighing options
rounds.scene_hint: career crossroads, loyalty vs opportunity, professional ethics

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Whistleblower Dilemma
rounds.story: You discover that a key business metric your company publicly reports — used by clients, partners, and possibly investors to make decisions — is being 'adjusted' to look better than the underlying data supports. It's not outright fraud, but it is materially misleading. Your manager seems aware and has not acted. You have documented evidence.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to what you've discovered
rounds.coaching_moment: The whistleblower scenario is the highest-stakes test of ethical reasoning in professional life. Most people talk about what they would do in the abstract; very few do it in practice. This scenario asks you to be honest about your actual instincts.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever known something was wrong and said nothing? What did it cost you internally? What would it have cost to speak?

choices.label: Escalate through internal channels — go above your manager to compliance, legal, or the CFO with your documented evidence
choices.feedback: Internal escalation with documented evidence is the appropriate first step — it gives the organisation a chance to self-correct before the matter reaches external stakeholders. It requires real courage, especially when your manager is complicit. But the alternative — silence — makes you complicit too. The evidence you've collected is the thing that protects you.
choices.coaching_moment: Internal escalation with documentation is not disloyalty — it's the most loyal thing you can do for an organisation you want to see succeed. Silence protects the individuals doing the wrong thing, not the organisation.

choices.label: Raise it directly with your manager again — give them another chance to act before escalating
choices.feedback: Giving your manager another opportunity is reasonable — but if they were already aware and didn't act, the second conversation is unlikely to produce a different outcome. The more important question is what you do if they again choose inaction. Going in without a clear answer to that question puts you in a weaker position.
choices.coaching_moment: A second conversation with someone who already knew and didn't act is not a bad move — but it needs a clear plan for what happens next if the answer is still no.

choices.label: Document what you know, protect yourself, but say nothing for now — the risk to your career is too high
choices.feedback: Documenting and staying silent is the most common response to this scenario — and it is understandable given the career risk. But it makes you a silent participant in what is happening, and the documentation you're keeping will eventually feel like evidence of what you knew and when. The cost of silence, carried internally, is also significant.
choices.coaching_moment: The belief that staying silent protects you is often wrong. Once you have documented knowledge of a material misrepresentation, silence is its own kind of exposure — moral and sometimes legal.

rounds.scene_hint: late night office, ethical weight, documented evidence, moment of reckoning

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

achievements.title: Professional Baseline Established
achievements.description: Completed the Professional Edition Soft Skills Baseline Assessment

transfer_exercises: This week, identify one conversation you've been deferring with a manager or team member. What is the cost of continuing to defer it?
Find one situation where someone on your team deserves explicit credit. Give it proactively — in writing, in a meeting, or to their manager.
Identify one organisational process or incentive that encourages the wrong behaviour. Write down how you would change it if you had the authority.
target_age: Working professionals, HR, trainers, and managers (ages 26+)
coaching_moment: Every choice shapes your strategy — great leaders think several steps ahead before deciding.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 4 rounds of Your Soft Skills Baseline — Professional Edition. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
